title: Why high-concept pitches ("iPhone for projectors") backfire and a clear positioning statement wins
summary: Jason Cohen argues against the "X is Y for Z" high-concept pitch because it is too brief, ambiguous, and defines you as a copy of something else. He prefers a clear positioning statement and a full product pitch, illustrated with a compact-projector example.

principles.text: Brevity has a limit: a three-word analogy to something famous leaves it unclear what message the listener receives.
principles.quote: When you use only three words and when you invoke something well-known and complicated, it's not clear what message will be received. I'm brevity's biggest fan, but there's such a thing as "too brief."

principles.text: Analogy pitches import every attribute of the referenced product, including its negatives, not just the ones you want.
principles.quote: But these aren't the only attributes of the iPhone. iPhones have a reputation of not working well with Microsoft Office, something particularly troubling for the traveling salesperson.

principles.text: Analogy pitches define you as a copy of something else; define yourself on your own terms.
principles.quote: And it defines you as a copy of something else.

principles.text: Use a one-line positioning statement that keeps the primary features and benefits as the guide for all marketing.
principles.quote: A compact, portable, rugged projector that eliminates surprises on the road.

principles.text: Think about your audience's existing associations: a traveling salesperson on PowerPoint and Outlook reads "iPhone" very differently than a Gmail user does.
principles.quote: Readers of this blog are likely to use GMail and Open Office, but your typical salesperson is on a strict diet of PowerPoint and Outlook.

principles.text: Investors need to understand product; strategy with zero product understanding isn't strategy, so steer clear of investors who think product is nothing.
principles.quote: Strategy with zero product understanding isn't strategy.
